newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't faces wrath over reform compromise.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't faces wrath over reform compromise.

text.p: Brazil's government faced strong criticism from members of its own alliance in Congress as well as the media on Thursday over a compromise that led to approval of a controversial bill to reform the civil service.
"Privileges for politicians allow the reform to pass," screamed the normally sedate Estado de Sao Paulo newspaper in its front-page headline.

Analysts said the one-vote margin of victory for the government when the Chamber of Deputies approved the bill late on Wednesday could spell trouble for President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's administration.

Cardoso, fearing defeat of one of his flagship reforms, announced shortly before the vote that the government would back an amendment exempting lawmakers and public sector workers from a pay ceiling included in the reform.

"That's the price to be paid for a reform which the country needs," Cardoso's spokesman told reporters, admitting the government had bowed to pressure within Congress. An estimated 140 lawmakers who receive pensions from previous civil service posts stood to lose out from the 10,800 reais ($10,188) ceiling on monthly pay and pension.
The amendment would allow elected officials and personal aides of senior civil servants to earn up to twice the amount.

"This is going to reflect very badly on Congress," said Artur Vigilio, general secretary of Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party. He said the party might vote against the amendment when it is voted on in the lower house next week.

Leaders of government-allied political parties met on Thursday to discuss the possibility of less controversial form of the amendment. But government officials shrugged off the outcry and said the amendment would reduce by $500 million the $18 billion the reform is expected to save the federal, state and municipal governments over the next five years.

The civil service reform bill is considered crucial to the government's attempts to narrow Brazil's public sector deficit -- equivalent to 3.89 percent of gross domestic product last year -- and build on nearly three years of low inflation.
